newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan forex deregulation spurs capital flows.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan forex deregulation spurs capital flows.

text.p: Tokyo's financial markets face a coming tide of foreign exchange deregulation likely to trigger massive capital flows that could drown some government-protected financial institutions, experts say.
The first wave comes when Japan makes its first drastic reform in 17 years of the Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Control Law, effective April 1, 1998.
A sweeping new law on the whole area of foreign exchange controls is expected to win final approval in parliament on Friday.
The reform is part of a "Big Bang" of comprehensive financial deregulations that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto wants in effect in Japan by 2001.
The new law will eliminate numerous anachronistic regulations on cross-border transactions and allow corporations and individuals to deal directly with overseas banks and brokers.
CROSS-BORDER CAPITAL FLOWS COULD INCREASE

"Cross-border capital flows would double or triple in magnitude, suggesting enormous demand for foreign exchange in Tokyo," said Yukuo Takahashi, managing director, global trading division, Chase Manhattan Bank.
"Japanese investors have until now been forced to dine in licenced-local-restaurants which offered poor services and food," he said in a colourful description of the way things are at present.
"But from April next year, all restaurants that pass sanitary standards will be able to operate in Tokyo."
But, the freedom to enter into a more lucrative foreign exchange market does not mean that everybody has a chance to flourish, Takahashi said.
In New York in the early 1980s, about 20 to 30 major forex players shared the market.
But, now there remain only five to six major players in the world's most liquid currency market.
There will be a similiar downsizing in Tokyo with inefficient operators closing shop, experts said.
Investors will select their bank of choice solely on the basis of how much expertise, information, risk management skills and other infrastructure they have.
The deregulation is likely to lead to changes in who are the major clients of banks.
The top 100 clients of the major U.S. banks were once trade-related customers, such as exporters and importers.
But now the top 100 are capital investors, such as mutual funds and hedge funds.

Tokyo's contentious current account surplus for fiscal 1996/97 was 7.18 trillion yen ($61.9 billion). The surplus accounts for a mere 0.6 percent of financial assets held by Japanese individual investors.
FOREIGN BANKS AND BROKERS SHOWING INTENSE INTEREST
Of 1,192 trillion yen worth of Japanese individual financial assets, 66.4 percent is held in low yielding yen deposits and cash.

Analysts expect individuals to begin shopping abroad more often for the cheapest and best financial services, and foreign banks and brokers are showing intense interest in getting a slice of the action.
However, monetary authorities do not seem worried about a capital flight spurred by individuals.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry of Finance (MOF) International Finance Bureau has said that he does not see a massive individual capital outflow gathering momentum.
"It's a question over the next several years of whether foreign mutual funds successfully market to individual investors here as part of the Big Bang."
LAW CHANGES SCENE FOR DIRECT INVESTMENT
The new law will also change the scene on direct investment in Japan.

"The new forex law will effectively ensure a money route for good venture capital, by eliminating most of the barriers to cross-border transactions," Takeshi Hanai, executive manager of the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's International Treasury Department.
Many venture capitalists are now struggling for funds and a lack of cash liquidity is choking business.
"Smooth cash flow to the right venture capitalists here will in turn stimulate the (Japanese) economy," Hanai said.
Foreign companies' direct investment in Japan for April-September, 1996 was 283.4 billion yen, or only one tenth of Japanese companies' direct investment in foreign nations of 2.66 trillion yen.
NEW LAW WILL LEAD TO STRUCTURAL REFORM
"The new law will undoubtedly make a breakthrough to the structural reform of Japan's economy," said Teruhiko Mano, adviser to the president of Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd.
"The goal of the new law is to smash the Japanese system that offers high-cost services and expensive goods," Mano said.
Nobody has been successful so far in destroying a high cost system that has survived on industries protected by politicians who received kick-backs for favourable treatment.
"The new forex law means that Japan will let the market mechanism challenge the decades-old system, via accelerating cross-border transactions in money," Mano said.
By doing so, price differentials for similar services provided by foreign and Japanese companies, will become known to all.
As a result, high commissions for foreign exchanges and stock deals, and various taxes on securities transactions will have to disappear, Mano said.
Japanese banks are among the most affected by the structural changes, he said.

Experts say forex liberalisation in April 1998 will cause bigger fundamental changes in the Japanese financial sector than the 1975 "May Day" reforms in the United States or the 1986 British "Big Bang."
ROLE OF MONETARY AUTHORITY WILL HAVE TO CHANGE
The role of monetary authorities will have to change along with the introduction of the new forex law, IBJ's Hanai said.
Monetary authorities will find it more difficult to exert influence via intervention in the forex market as it grows in depth and volume.
"The Bank of Japan (BOJ) will be tapping the market more regularly, as the German Bundesbank does, and placing commercial orders instead of interventions (with policy implications)," Hanai said.
They may even set a mild reference range for the dollar/yen to ensure currency stability for businesses. ($ = 115.9 Japanese Yen)
